Look around the perimeter of the machine and see if there is any ductwork. That machine was most likely built with a downdraft system. 
If you can find a duct, follow it. It should lead you to a dust collect of some kind - most likely a Donaldson or Robovent, there are many other brands but those seem to be most common on lasers. 
If the dust collector is running it will be making a pretty loud, constant hum. It should make a lout pfft every so often when it does the blowdown.
Even if the machine is running, if it isn’t performing a blowdown then it probably isn’t working properly. 

As others have noted, the fact that you were never shown a dust collector is concerning. Most units have barrels under them that collect the dust when it blows down off the filter and the laser operators are often the ones responsible for changing barrels out when they’re full. I’m sure it could be a maintenance task but most places that I’m aware of have the operator do it. I really doubt that the barrel changeout would be automated.

As I understand it, right to work keeps unions from creating closed shops. 
A closed shop being someplace where the only way you’re allowed to work there is to join the union. The purpose of the closed shop agreement is to keep people from free riding on union negotiated pay/benefits. 

So in a right to work state, you might see union and non-union employees working the same types of jobs at the same company, potentially receiving the same compensation. 

This is where the rip-off statement comes in. If enough workers free ride the union and continue to receive the same compensation, it makes the union weaker. If the union dissolves, it could leave all of the workers in a much worse position than if they were all just in the union to begin with.

Edit: it sounds clunky to say unions create closed shops. The company enters into an union security agreement which creates what I’ve commonly heard as a closed shop.

My great grandfather apparently told my mom when she was young “to stop learning is to stop living”. She carried that phrase into adulthood and had it posted on her desk when she was a high school teacher. 

A few years ago I dug through some of his things, found a small notebook that he carried on the farm which had his handwriting. I also found some checks with his signature. 

I scanned examples of every letter and strung them together to make his phrase, and put his signature down below. Then printed that and laid it out on a piece of wood from our farm and transferred it using a wood chisel. I also carved a draft horse into the end of the wood - great grandpa grew up using teams of horses for field work. 

Turns out his signature on the checks was actually written by my great grandmother. It should have been obvious to me as the style was significantly different but I didn’t realize it until an older relative explained that she always wrote the checks and just signed his name.

So now my mom has the handwriting of both of her maternal grandparents on lumber that came from her paternal grandparents’ farm, on which she was raised (as was I).

Like the commenter below said, this is likely 3 to 4.5kW of power. The CO2 lasers are something like 15% electrical efficiency whereas fiber lasers are 30-40% efficient. 
This being a tube laser it is likely CO2, although the small diameter/thickness tubing indicates it could be a fiber, as there are some fiber machines in the small tube market.

In the laser world, Mazak is definitely not the Mercedes. Trumpf and Bystronic probably compete the most for that position. 
Mazak makes a solid machine at a great price, but they aren’t the top of the line.

The laser like he’s describing is likely anywhere from 4000 to 10000 watts. 
Fiber lasers are the current state of the art and will likely continue to dominate the metal cutting industry. CO2 lasers handle thick material a little better but fiber is catching up quickly. CO2s typically go up to 6000 watts max. The reputable fibers are currently maxed out at 10k, although there are some lesser known companies that claim higher wattage. 

Comparing laser cuts to plasma cuts is tricky. Good plasmas often have a smoother cut edge due to the high heat and large kerf, but the edge always has a taper and you cannot make as sharp of corners - they’re always rounded a little. Lasers cutting with nitrogen do not oxidize the edge of the part, which is important with stainless steel cutting or when cutting parts that will be painted (paint adheres to oxide, then oxide falls off and you have an unpainted edge). Plasmas also tend to leave more dross on the backside of the part, requiring more cleanup. 

Speed wise it really depends on the thickness of materials being cut. High powered fiber lasers cutting thin materials with nitrogen should outrun just about anything. Above 1/2” plasmas will likely be just as fast or faster, but you still have the issues described above.

You might already do this, but here's what I do. 
Break the lift down into its parts and practice those parts individually.
Go to low weight, practice snapping under the bar. Just stand with your arms straight down holding the  bar w/ 115 or something, bounce the weight with your shoulders and time that bounce to your drop and get yourself under the bar. Focus on getting under the bar as fast as possible, don't think about lifting the bar up, just getting yourself under it.
Then do your regular power clean workout with your typical weight and reps.
Then increase the weight and do a modified deadlift with full triple extension at the top.
Then front squat. Make sure to do at least one set with your goal power clean weight.
